title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
text:
Topic 1 · Prompting as specification
Guiding question: if the assistant builds exactly what you asked, why does it so often build the wrong thing?
In session 1 your team wrote a brief and had a working page in under an hour. The second hour usually feels different: the assistant adds a button you never asked for, the list sorts the wrong way, “save” works on your laptop and not on your phone. None of that is the assistant being careless. It is the assistant filling the gaps you left with the most common answer from millions of other apps. A quote tool for a food distributor in Chile is not the most common app.
The fix is a habit, not a tool. Before you ask for a feature, write it as a user story with acceptance criteria. A user story is one sentence: as a sales rep, I want to paste a customer message and save it as a quote request, so that I stop retyping it into the ERP. Acceptance criteria are the three to six checks that tell you, and the assistant, when the story is done. With fewer than three you leave the decisions to the assistant. With more than six you have probably glued two stories together.








Part
Weak
Strong




User
“users”
“a Cerro Azul sales rep on a phone, between customer visits”


Action
“handle quotes”
“paste a WhatsApp message and save it as a quote request for one named customer”


Done when
“it works”
“the request appears at the top of the list with date, rep and customer; empty messages are refused”



Managers know this format from product teams. What is new is that the assistant reads it literally. Each criterion you write is one decision it does not have to guess. Each one you leave out is a surprise waiting in the next hour.







In the business



Paula retyping a quote costs Cerro Azul about 12 minutes. A manager who specifies badly costs more: every vague request is a build, a test, a complaint and a rebuild. The assistant is cheap per attempt, but your team’s two hours in the lab are not. Acceptance criteria are the cheapest insurance you will buy in this course.




Practice · Topic 1

Which of these is an acceptance criterion, as opposed to a wish?

The quote tool should be fast, clear and easy for reps to use on a phone between visits.
An empty message cannot be saved; the save button stays disabled until there is text.
As a rep, I want to save quote requests quickly so that I stop retyping them into the ERP.

A criterion is a check that is either true or false when you use the app. "Cannot be saved when empty" is one. "Fast and easy" is a wish, and the assistant will decide for you what it means.


The assistant added a "priority" dropdown to the quote request that nobody asked for. What most likely happened?

The assistant could not build the fields you asked for, so it replaced them with something it could build.
Your story did not list the fields of a quote request, so the assistant used the usual ones from similar apps.
The assistant has its own plan for what the app should become and is quietly adding features toward that plan.

Every unspecified field is a guess. Listing the fields (customer, message, date, rep, status) in the criteria removes the guess, and the dropdown.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
section: Topic 2 · Small steps, checkpoints and undo
text:
Topic 2 · Small steps, checkpoints and undo
Guiding question: how do you make it safe, and fast, to break the app?
Every first-time builder repeats one pattern. Confidence is high, so the team pastes a single request: login, customer list, quote form, PDF export, email notification, dashboard. The assistant produces something that mostly runs. Then the login breaks the list, the PDF breaks the form, and nobody knows which of the six changes caused which of the four problems.
The alternative is boring and it works: one story per request. Ask for the customer picker. Use the app as Paula would, in a phone-sized window on your laptop (your browser can show any page at a phone’s width). If it works, save a checkpoint. If it does not, you know what broke, because only one thing changed.

The rule has a second half: test by using, not by reading. You are not going to read the code and you do not need to. Do the rep’s task end to end, including the cases that should fail. When something looks wrong, ask: what did you change and why? The answer is written in plain language, and it is often where you find the gap in your criteria.
Small steps are only cheap if going back is cheap. Software teams solve that with version control (the usual tool is Git, with the history kept online on GitHub). You will use it through the assistant, so you need three ideas, not the commands:

A checkpoint (a commit) is a named snapshot of the whole app at a moment it worked. In this course, saving a checkpoint always includes sending it to GitHub, which is what updates your public address a minute later. “Customer picker working” is a good name. Save one after every story that passes your test, and at least every 20 minutes.
A branch is an experiment: a copy where you try something risky without touching the version that works. If it is good you merge it. If not, you discard it and nothing happened.
Rollback returns the app to any earlier checkpoint, in seconds. The worst case of a bad request becomes “go back twenty minutes”.

Rollback has a limit worth knowing before you rely on it. It restores the code. It does not restore what is in the database, emails that were already sent, or what customers already saw. A change that deletes or rewrites data needs its own care: ask the assistant what the change does to existing rows before you approve it.
You ask for all of it in plain language: save a checkpoint called “login working”, start a branch to try a new layout, go back to the checkpoint before the PDF export.
That gives every test in the lab one of two places. On your laptop, before the checkpoint: the app runs on your own machine and only you can see it. At the public address, after the checkpoint: a phone or a second device can open it, about a minute later. A test on a real phone always belongs to the second kind.







In the business



This is how good operations teams already work: change one thing on the line, measure, keep or revert. The history is also your audit trail. When Diego asks why the discount field disappeared last Tuesday, the timeline answers in one click, and when you hand the prototype to engineering in session 4, the record of what was tried and why is worth more to them than the code.



Practice · Topic 2

After one request for three features, the quote list stopped loading. You described the bug precisely once and the fix did not work. What is the fastest way forward?

Read through the code the assistant wrote for the three features until you spot the line that is wrong.
Roll back to the last checkpoint and ask for the three features again one at a time, testing after each.
Describe the bug again in other words and keep asking for fixes until the list loads as it did before.

One precise description is worth trying: a bug is a conversation. When that fails on a tangle of changes, going back to the last state that worked and adding the changes one by one isolates the cause in minutes. This is why checkpoints and small steps belong together.


When should your team save a checkpoint?

At the end of each working day, with the date in the name so that the history reads like a calendar.
After every story that passes your test, with a name that says what works, and at least every 20 minutes.
After every single request to the assistant, whether or not the result passed your test, to lose nothing.

A checkpoint is a state you would be happy to return to. Name it after what works, so rolling back is a choice between meaningful states and not between timestamps.


Diego wants to try a radical redesign of the quote list while Paula's login story is half built. What should he do?

Start a branch for the redesign, so the working version and the login work stay untouched until it is merged.
Make the changes directly in the working version, since the assistant can always repair what the redesign breaks.
Copy the whole project to another folder on his laptop and build the redesign there, away from Paula's work.

A branch is exactly this: an experiment that cannot break the working app. Merge it when it passes the test, or discard it at no cost.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
text:
Topic 3 · Where the data lives
Guiding question: why did the quote requests disappear when Paula refreshed the page?
QuoteDesk v0 kept its quote requests in the page: they existed only in the browser that created them, as “today’s list on that device”. Refresh, and they are gone. Open the app on Diego’s phone, and the list is empty. That is normal for a first hour and useless for a second rep.
Data can live in three places. In the page: instant, free, gone on refresh. In a file on the server: survives refresh, but two reps saving at once can overwrite each other and nothing says who is who. In a managed database: a service that stores rows, serves many users at once, keeps backups, and comes with authentication (the login: who are you) built in. For anything two people will use, the database is the answer, and the assistant sets it up in a few requests.
The login matters beyond security. It ties each quote request to the rep who created it, and it lets the app have two roles from today: rep and manager, with Carla’s account as the manager. In v1 the quote requests are a shared queue that every signed-in rep sees, so that anyone can pick up a waiting customer. Priced quotes, with their discounts, will be private to the rep who owns the customer and to Carla. That second rule is not built by a login; it is the subject of session 4.







In the business



“Where does the data live?” is the first question legal, IT and finance will ask, long before they ask what the app does. “In a managed database, in a named region, with a login per rep” is the answer that lets a prototype be piloted with real customers. “On my laptop” is the answer that ends the meeting.



Practice · Topic 3

Paula and Diego save quote requests at the same moment. Which storage choice handles this safely?

In the page, held in each rep's browser memory.
In one shared file kept on the server.
In a managed database with a login per rep.

A managed database is built for many people writing at once and records who created each row. The other two break as soon as there is a second person.


QuoteDesk v1 has a login. Marcos signs in. What has the app established?

Who he is, so what he saves is tied to him. What he may see is a separate rule still to be written.
That he can see only his own customers' priced quotes, because the login filters everything by rep.
That everything he types is encrypted, so nobody else at Cerro Azul or outside can read his quotes.

Authentication answers "who are you". Authorization answers "what may you do". QuoteDesk v1 needs the first; assuming it gives you the second is the mistake session 4 opens with.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
section: Topic 4 · UX for output that is sometimes wrong
text:
Topic 4 · UX for output that is sometimes wrong
Guiding question: Paula will trust QuoteDesk once. What makes her trust it the second time?
Next session QuoteDesk will read a pasted message and propose the items: 20 cajas of aceite 900 cc, 5 sacos of arroz, “lo de siempre de lácteos”. The last one is a guess. If the app shows that guess with the same confidence as the first two, Paula learns after one wrong delivery that nothing on the screen can be trusted. Then she checks every line, and the app saves nobody any time.
Four patterns fix this. They are decisions you write into the story, not into the code:

Show confidence. Lines the model is unsure about look different and say why.
Stream the result. Items appear as they are produced, so a three-second wait looks like progress and not like a frozen screen.
Honest errors. When there is nothing to extract, the app says “no items found in this message” and offers the manual form, not an empty table.
Let the user correct. Every proposed line can be edited in place and the correction is saved. The app is never the last word.

The model will be wrong some of the time whatever you do. The experience decides whether being wrong costs a glance or costs a customer.







In the business



Trust can be measured: how often reps edit a proposed line, how often they give up and retype, how many wrong deliveries trace back to a quote. Once reps use the tool, the correction button gives you that data for free, and the corrections become new examples for the test set you start in session 3.




Practice · Topic 4

The model is unsure what "lo de siempre de lácteos" means for Doña Elsa. What should the screen do?

Show the best guess as a normal line like the others, so the screen stays clean and quick to scan.
Show the guess marked as uncertain, with the reason, and make it one tap to confirm or to edit it.
Leave the line out of the proposal altogether, so that nothing wrong can ever be shown to the rep.

Visible uncertainty plus an easy correction is the pattern. Paula spends two seconds on the one line that needs her and trusts the rest.


A customer writes only "hola, me llamas?". What should QuoteDesk show?

An empty items table with the usual columns, ready for the rep to fill in by hand.
A red banner saying that something went wrong and asking the rep to try again later.
That no items were found, with the manual form and a call-back note one tap away.

An honest error says what happened and what the user can do next. It keeps Paula inside the tool.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
section: Topic 5 · Teach the assistant how you work: project instructions and skills
text:
Topic 5 · Teach the assistant how you work: project instructions and skills
Guiding question: you have explained Cerro Azul's quote format to the assistant four times this week. Where should that explanation live so that you never type it again?

Three things people call “the AI”
Before teaching “the assistant” anything, be exact about which one. From this session on, three different things are in play, and most confusion in AI projects comes from blurring them.










What it is
Who uses it
What it can reach




The building assistant
The agentic coding assistant your team builds QuoteDesk with
Your team, while building
The repository and its project instructions, plus the assistant’s own skills and connectors


A rep’s assistant
The assistant Paula or Carla uses directly for daily work: drafting a quote, summarizing calls, the morning digest
A rep or a manager, every day
The same skills and connectors, with that person’s own access. Not the project instructions


The model inside QuoteDesk
The model that the deployed app calls through an API (an API is the door through which one program asks another for a service)
Nobody directly; the app calls it
Only what the app sends it, and only the tools the app defines. No skills, no connectors



In this course one assistant app plays both parts: opened on the repository it is the building assistant; opened anywhere else it is your rep’s assistant.
The consequence matters for your milestone. Everything in this topic and the next extends the first two, never the deployed app. The project instructions belong to the repository and reach only the building assistant. The skill and the connector you deliver in M2 belong to the assistant itself and work in any conversation. QuoteDesk cannot open a skill or pass through a connector. In session 3 it gets its prices from its own products table, imported from the price sheet.


Project instructions and skills
The assistant starts every session knowing nothing about Cerro Azul. It does not know that a quote request is not a quote, that a caja of aceite holds 12 bottles, or that only Carla approves discounts. So far you have repeated these things in every prompt. There are two better places to put them, and they do different jobs.
Project instructions are a plain-text file in the project that the assistant reads at the start of every session. Different tools give it different names (for example CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md); the idea is the same. It holds what is always true: what the product is, your vocabulary, the rules (“one story per change”, “all money in CLP without decimals”, “ask before touching the login”) and how you want changes reported. Because it is always loaded, every line is paid for in every session. Keep it under a page. It lives in the repository, so only the building assistant reads it.
Skills hold procedures that are needed only sometimes. A skill is a folder with a file called SKILL.md: a name, a one-line description that says when to use it, and the steps. It can carry other files too: a template, examples, even small scripts. The assistant sees only the names and descriptions of your skills until a request matches one, and then it opens that folder and follows it. This is called progressive disclosure, and it is why twenty installed skills cost almost nothing until one is used. The format was published as an open standard in December 2025 and dozens of assistants and coding tools support it, so a skill written for one tool usually works in another. In this course you keep your skill among the assistant’s own skills, not inside the QuoteDesk repository, so that it is available in any conversation.










Loaded
Good for
At Cerro Azul




A prompt
Once, now
A one-off request
“Summarize yesterday’s calls”


Project instructions
Every session, always
Rules and vocabulary that never change
“Money in CLP, no decimals. Never change the login without asking.”


A skill
Only when a request matches its description
A procedure with steps, a template and examples
“How we write a quote”, “the Monday sales note”



One detail decides whether a skill works: the description is the trigger. It is the only part the assistant reads before choosing. “Formats quotes” gives it nothing to match. “Drafts or checks a Cerro Azul quote in the house format. Use whenever the user asks for a quote, cotización or price offer for a customer” tells it what the skill does and when to open it. Try both below.

One caution for later. A skill from the internet is a stranger’s instructions, and sometimes a stranger’s code, running with your access. Read it yourself before you install it; the assistant may help you read it, but its verdict is not the control. Session 4 treats this as what it is: a supply chain.






In the business



A skill is how know-how stops living in Paula’s head. When Carla changes the discount rule, she edits one file and every assistant that has the skill installed follows the new rule from the next request. That is process documentation that executes itself, and it deserves what any process document gets: an owner, a date, and a review when the process changes.



Practice · Topic 5

"All money in CLP without decimals. Never change the login without asking first." Where do these two rules belong?

In a skill called house-rules, so that they sit with the other procedures of the team.
In the project instructions file, because they apply to every request in the project.
At the top of every prompt, typed again each time, so the assistant always sees them.

What is always true goes in project instructions, which are always loaded. What is needed sometimes, and has steps, goes in a skill.


Your team installed the quote-format skill. Paula asks her assistant for a quote for Doña Elsa and gets a generic letter with an invented 5% discount. What is the most likely cause?

The skill's instructions are too long, so the assistant stopped reading before reaching the template.
The description does not say when to use the skill, so the assistant never opened the folder.
The model is too small for this task, so it could not follow a format with that many columns.

The description is the trigger. If the skill is right and the output ignores it, fix the description first: say what the skill does and when to use it, in the words a rep would use.


Diego finds a "sales-email-writer" skill online with thousands of downloads and wants to install it for the team. What comes first?

Open the folder and read SKILL.md and any script in it, as you would read a contract before signing.
Install it for the team now: thousands of downloads mean that many people have already checked it.
Ask the assistant whether the skill is safe, and install it for the team if the answer is yes.

A skill is instructions, and sometimes code, that will act with your permissions. It is short enough to read in five minutes. Read it yourself, and prefer writing your own for anything that touches customers.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
section: Topic 6 · Connect the assistant to your systems: connectors and MCP
text:
Topic 6 · Connect the assistant to your systems: connectors and MCP
Guiding question: the price list lives in Drive and the customers live in the ERP. How does your team's assistant reach them without you copying and pasting?
Until now the assistant has known only what you pasted into it. Ask it what aceite 900 cc costs for Minimarket Los Aromos and it has two honest options: say it does not know, or guess. The answer sits in two systems it cannot see.
A connector gives the assistant a door into one of those systems. Underneath, most connectors use the same open standard, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced in late 2024 and since handed to a neutral foundation, so that a connector built once works with many assistants. Each system is presented by a small program called a server, which offers three things:








A server offers
Which means
At Cerro Azul




Tools
Actions the assistant can ask for
“look up a price”, “find a customer”, “send an email”


Resources
Data it can read
the price list, the delivery policy document


Prompts
Ready-made requests
“weekly price changes”



You rarely build one. For Drive, email, calendars, the common CRMs and databases they already exist, and in most assistants you switch them on in a settings screen. Signing in uses the “Sign in with…” window you already know (the standard is called OAuth), and it has a consequence worth saying aloud: the assistant gets at most the access of the person who signed in, narrowed by the permissions the connector asks for. If Paula cannot open the payroll folder, neither can her assistant. What Paula can open, her assistant can usually open too. One exception to watch: a connector set up with a shared service account gives everyone who uses it that account’s access, whoever they are.
That makes every connector a decision about access. Three rules cover most of it:

Read before write. A connector that can only read can produce a wrong answer. One that can send or write can produce a wrong action.
One system at a time. Add a door, use it for a week, then add the next. If five open at once you cannot tell which one caused the problem.
What comes back is data, not instructions. A document or an email fetched through a connector may contain text that looks like an order. Session 4 shows what happens when the assistant obeys it.

Skills and connectors complement each other. The skill is how we write a quote. The connector is where the prices are. With both, Paula’s one-line request to her assistant produces a quote in the house format with prices read from the list, not guessed. Remember whose doors these are: they belong to the team’s assistants. The deployed QuoteDesk does not pass through them.







In the business



A manager should be able to say, in one sentence, which systems the assistant can read, which it can change, and who approved that. Start with the price list, read-only: the worst case is a wrong number on Paula’s screen, with the source one click away. Email and ERP orders are a different conversation, and they come with approval in session 3 and with permissions in session 4.



Practice · Topic 6

Paula's assistant now drafts quotes in the right house format, but the prices are invented. What is missing?

A better description on the skill, so that the assistant finds the prices inside the template.
A connector to the price list, so that the assistant reads the prices and does not guess them.
A larger model, because bigger models have seen more price lists and guess them more accurately.

The skill is how; the connector is where. Invented prices mean the assistant has the procedure and no access to the data.


Which connector should the team switch on first for its assistants?

ERP orders with write access, because creating the order is where most of the reps' time is saved.
All five at once, so the team sees in one afternoon everything that the assistant is able to do.
The price list, read-only: useful today, and the worst case is a wrong answer that Paula can check.

Read before write, one system at a time. Pick the door with the most value and the smallest worst case, and open the next one after a week of use.


Paula connects her assistant to Drive by signing in with her own account. What can the assistant read?

Everything in Cerro Azul's Drive, because the connector belongs to the company account.
At most what Paula herself can open, which may be far more than the price list.
Only the price list, because that is the one file she asked the assistant about.

The assistant can reach at most what Paula can open, narrowed by the permissions the connector asks for. If that is too wide, share a single folder with a dedicated account, or limit the connector to that folder.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
section: Build lab · QuoteDesk v1, one skill, one connector
text:
Build lab · QuoteDesk v1, one skill, one connector

What your team builds in the next 120 minutes
Teams of 2 to 3 · the instructor circulates · minutes in parentheses are a guide and include a 10-minute break · save a checkpoint after every story that passes, and at least every 20 minutes · a checkpoint always goes to GitHub

Watch the live demo (10). The instructor adds the database and the login to a v0 in two separate requests, tests each on the laptop, saves a checkpoint, and shows the public address updating. One change goes wrong on purpose and is rolled back.
Open the project you prepared (5). Before class you followed the setup guide: QuoteDesk v0 is in a GitHub repository, it opens in the building assistant, and an empty database project exists. Confirm that the repository is private. Ask the assistant to save a first checkpoint called "v0 from session 1" and check that it appears in the repository's history. If your setup is not finished, tell the instructor now and start from the template repository.
Write the project instructions file (10). Use the first prompt below. Read what the assistant proposes, cut it to under 40 lines, and save it. From now on you stop repeating these rules.
Write the first story with criteria (10). In your shared document, write the user story for saving a quote request with 3 to 6 acceptance criteria: the fields, the rules, the failure case, the device. Paste it as one request. Nothing else in the same message.
Test by using, then checkpoint (10). On your laptop: paste a realistic message with names, phone numbers and addresses changed, pick a customer, save. Try an empty message. Try it in a phone-sized window on your laptop. If something fails, ask "what did you change and why?" and fix the criteria before asking for a fix. When it passes, save a checkpoint named after what works, wait for the public address to update, and repeat the test there on a real phone.
Add the database (10). Use the database prompt below: quote requests go into the database project from the setup guide, with the same fields. The project address and the publishable key are already in the project's settings, and the secret key is only on the hosting platform, so nobody pastes a key into the chat. Test on your laptop: save, refresh, the request is still there. Save the checkpoint "database working". Then open the public address on a second device: the request is there too.
Add the login, as its own request (15). Use the login prompt below: sign-in with email and password, a password reset, two roles (rep and manager, with Carla's account as the manager), and each request tied to the rep who created it. The same prompt turns on row-level rules, so that the database itself refuses anyone who is not signed in; ask to see the refusals. Test on your laptop with two rep accounts and signed out. Save the checkpoint "login working", then sign in at the public address from a phone.
Break (10). Stand up. Leave the laptop open on the last checkpoint.
Break something on purpose, roll back, try a branch (10). Ask for a risky change you do not need, such as "replace the list with a calendar view". Confirm on your laptop that it changed something you did not want, roll back to the last checkpoint and confirm the app is exactly as before, and notice that the requests in the database were not touched by the rollback. Then let one teammate try a new list layout on a branch, and merge it only if it passes the test. The rollback counts for M2: the repository history must show it.
Apply two UX patterns (5). In one request, add the honest empty state ("no requests yet, paste a message to start") and a loading state while the queue is fetched. Note in your build log which patterns from topic 4 you chose and why.
Create the quote-format skill and prove it triggers (10). Use the skill prompt below with your own format. It is a personal skill of your assistant, not a folder in the QuoteDesk repository. Start a new conversation outside the repository, ask for a quote without mentioning the skill, and check that the output follows your template. Take a screenshot for M2. Then ask for something unrelated and check that the skill stays closed.
Connect the price list, read-only (10). Put your price list in a shared folder (a sheet with 20 rows is enough, with invented prices if yours are confidential), switch on the connector for it in your assistant with read access only, and run the connector test prompt. Check the answer against the sheet with your own eyes and take a screenshot for M2.
Check the public address and share (5). Confirm that the public address shows your last checkpoint (the hosting section of the setup guide explains how it updates), open it on a phone, and paste the address, the repository link and the checkpoint list into your team's M2 document.


Six prompts to adapt. Start with the difference between a request that produces surprises and the same story written so the assistant does not have to guess.

Weak requestAdd a way to save quote requests and make a nice list. Also add login and a database and make it work on mobile.
Strong requestOne story, with the fields, the rules, the failure case and the device named. The database comes as its own request after this one passes, and the login after that.

You, to the assistant · project instructions (step 3)Create the project instructions file for this repository, using the file name you read at the start of every session. Keep it under 40 lines. Include:

What this is: QuoteDesk, an internal tool for Cerro Azul's 14 sales reps to turn pasted customer messages into quote requests.
Vocabulary: a quote request is the customer's message saved against a customer; a quote is the priced answer. Keep product units as written (caja, saco); never convert them.
Rules: one user story per change. Do not add features I did not ask for. All money in CLP without decimals. Dates as day-month-year. Ask before changing the login or the structure of the database. Never write a key or a password into a file. Use only invented or de-identified customer data. After each story I confirm works, save a checkpoint named after what works. A checkpoint means: commit and push to GitHub. Tell me when the public address has updated.
Reporting: after every change, tell me in plain language what you changed and how to test it on my laptop, in a phone-sized window.

Show me the file before you save it.
You, to the assistant · story 1 (step 4)User story: as a Cerro Azul sales rep using a phone between visits, I want to paste a customer's WhatsApp message and save it as a quote request for one customer, so that I stop retyping it into the ERP.

Acceptance criteria:
1. The customer is chosen from the existing customer list (search by name), not typed freely.
2. A quote request has: customer, pasted message, date and time created, rep name, status "new".
3. The save button is disabled while the message is empty.
4. After saving, the request appears at the top of the list with customer, date and the first line of the message.
5. The list and the form work on a phone screen without sideways scrolling.

Build only this. When done, tell me in plain language what you changed.
You, to the assistant · database (step 6, after story 1 passes)Store quote requests in the database project that is already connected to this repository, with the same fields: customer, message, date and time created, rep name, status. The project address and the publishable key are in the project's settings; the publishable key may reach the browser. Do not ask me for any secret key and do not use one. Do not change the form or the list. Build only this, and tell me how to test it on my laptop, and then from a second device at the public address.
The assistant, a good replyDone. Quote requests are now saved in the database with the five fields you listed. I used the project address and the publishable key from the project's settings and no secret key. To test on your laptop: save a request and refresh, it is still there. I did not touch the form or the list. Tell me when it passes and I will save the checkpoint "database working" and push it to GitHub. About a minute later, open the public address on a second device: the request is there too.

You, to the assistant · login (step 7, after the database passes)Add sign-in for reps with email and password, and a password reset. There are two roles: rep and manager. Carla's account is the manager; every other account is a rep. Each quote request is tied to the rep who created it and shows that rep's name. After signing in, every rep sees the shared queue of quote requests, newest at the top. Someone who is not signed in sees only the sign-in screen. Then turn on row-level rules in the database so that every table refuses reads and writes when nobody is signed in. Run that test and show me the refusals. Do not change the form or the layout of the list. Build only this, and tell me how to test it on my laptop with two rep accounts and signed out.
The assistant, a good replyDone. I added sign-in with email and password and a reset link, and two roles: Carla's account is the manager, the others are reps. Each saved request carries the signed-in rep and shows the name in the queue. To test: create two rep accounts, save one request from each, and confirm both appear in the queue under the right name; then sign out and confirm you see only the sign-in screen. I turned on row-level rules: with no signed-in user, reading and writing the quote requests table are both refused, and the two refusals are shown below. I did not touch the form or the layout. Tell me when it passes and I will save the checkpoint "login working" and push it.
You, to the assistant · the skill (step 11)Create a skill called quote-format as a personal skill of this assistant, not inside the QuoteDesk repository, so that it is available in any conversation.

Description, written so that you will find it: "Drafts or checks a Cerro Azul quote in the house format. Use whenever I ask for a quote, cotización or price offer for a customer, or paste a quote request."

Instructions:
1. Use the customer name I give you. If I give none, stop and ask me.
2. One line per product: code, name, quantity, unit, list price in CLP.
3. Mark any line you are not sure about with CHECK and say why.
4. Never apply a discount. Discounts need Carla's approval.
5. Fill template.md and compare with the example before answering.

Add template.md with our header, the product lines and the delivery note, and one worked example made from the request I paste below. Then tell me how to check, in a new conversation, that the skill loads without my naming it.
You, to the assistant · connector test (step 12)Using the price list connector, tell me the list price of aceite 900 cc, caja de 12, and name the file and the row where you found it. Do not change anything in the file. If you cannot find the product, say so. Do not estimate a price.
Your lab checklist. It stays saved in this browser.

The project is in a private repository, opens in the building assistant, and has a first checkpoint.
The project instructions file exists, is under 40 lines, and the team has read it.
Story 1 was written with 3 to 6 acceptance criteria before asking the assistant.
Story 1 was tested on the laptop with a realistic message (names, phone numbers and addresses changed) and an empty message, then on a phone at the public address.
Quote requests are in the database: they survive a refresh and show on a second device.
Sign-in works with two rep accounts, signed-out visitors see nothing, each request shows its rep, and the database itself refuses a request with no signed-in user.
One risky change was made on purpose and rolled back to a checkpoint.
One experiment was tried on a branch and merged or discarded.
The honest empty state and the loading state are in the app.
The quote-format skill triggers in a new conversation without being named, and stays closed for an unrelated request.
One connector is on in the team's assistant, read-only, and its answer was checked against the source.
The public address shows the last checkpoint and opens on a phone, no secret key was pasted into a chat, and every build log is up to date.

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
text:
Critique and reflection
Two teams show one user story end to end: paste a message, pick the customer, save, refresh, sign in as a second rep. The class then asks each presenting team for two things live: roll back one change, and make the quote-format skill trigger without naming it. The rubric criterion in focus this session is functionality: does the product work for its user end to end, including the cases that should fail?
Reflection prompt for your build log: what did the assistant guess that you should have specified, and which line would you now add to your acceptance criteria, your project instructions or your skill?

title: Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
Class 2 · Specify, iterate, keep what works
text:
Summary

The assistant builds what you specify and guesses the rest. Three to six acceptance criteria remove the guesses.
One story per request. Test by using, not by reading. Ask “what did you change and why?”
A checkpoint is a state that worked, with a name, sent to GitHub; that is what updates the public address. Test on your laptop before it and at the public address after it. A branch is an experiment that cannot break the working app. Rollback makes small steps cheap, and it restores the code, not the data or the emails already sent.
Data for two or more people belongs in a managed database with a login. Authentication is “who are you”; authorization comes in session 4.
Four UX patterns for output that is sometimes wrong: visible confidence, streaming, honest errors, user correction.
Three things are called “the AI”: the building assistant, a rep’s assistant, and the model inside QuoteDesk. Project instructions live in the repository and reach only the building assistant. Skills and connectors belong to the assistant and work in any conversation. None of them reaches the deployed app.
Project instructions hold what is always true and are always loaded, so keep them short. A skill holds a procedure and is opened only when a request matches its description. The description is the trigger.
A connector is a door into one system, with at most the access of whoever signed in. Read before write, one system at a time, and treat what comes back as data.

title: Security checklist
text:
You do not need to read code to run this list. Each check is something you do in a browser, or a question you put to your building assistant together with the proof you should ask for. An answer of “yes, it is secure” is not proof. Ask to be shown.
Run the checks on your own app before session 4 and note, for each one, pass, fail or could not tell. “Could not tell” is a finding. In the session 4 lab you fix the failures with your team. Your check marks are saved in this browser.

title: Security checklist
text:
Keys and secrets

No secret key reaches the browser. Ask: "List every key this app uses. For each one say whether it is publishable or secret, and show me where it is stored. Then search everything the browser downloads and prove no secret key appears in it."
No secret key is in the repository or its history. Ask: "Search this repository, including earlier versions, for anything that looks like a key or password. List what you find."
Any key that ever leaked was revoked. If the answer to either question above was yes, the key is revoked in the service's dashboard and replaced. Deleting the line is not enough.

title: Security checklist
section: Who can see and do what
text:
Who can see and do what


Nothing works without signing in. Open the app's address in a private browser window. You should reach the sign-in page and nothing else.
The database refuses strangers. Ask: "Show me, table by table, that a request with no signed-in user is refused for reading and for writing. Run the test and show me the refusals."
One user cannot open another user's private records. Sign in as one user, open a private record, copy its address, sign in as a second user, paste the address. You should be refused. Then ask the assistant to prove the same refusal at the database, not only on the screen.
Roles are enforced on the server. Sign in as an ordinary user and try the action only a manager may take. Ask: "Where is this rule checked? Show me that it is checked on the server and not only by hiding the button."

title: Security checklist
section: What the model is allowed to do
text:
What the model is allowed to do

A message cannot give orders. Paste a test message that contains an instruction, for example a line asking for a discount on everything. The app should treat it as text to process and should not act on it.
The model can only return what the app expects. Ask: "What exactly can the model return to this app? Show me that anything outside that shape is rejected." A free-text answer that the app then acts on is a finding.
Every action that reaches a customer or moves money waits for a person. List the actions your app can take on its own. For each, ask who approves it.
Every connector and tool has the least permission that works. For each one write: what it can read, what it can change, and whether the job would still get done with less.

title: Security checklist
text:
Data, cost and recovery

You can list the personal data the app holds. One line each: what it is, why you need it, how long you keep it, which outside provider sees it.
There is a spending limit and someone is told when it is reached. Find the limit in the model provider's dashboard. If there is none, that is a finding.
You can go back. Name the last checkpoint that worked and confirm you know how to return to it. Remember what going back does not undo: data already changed and messages already sent.

title: Security checklist
text:
What to bring to session 4
A single page with the fourteen checks and, next to each, pass, fail or could not tell, plus one sentence for every item that is not a pass. That page is the source for the findings section of your risk memo; attach it to your build log.

title: Toolkit setup guide
text:
This guide gets your tools ready. It is written for someone who has never programmed. The exact names of buttons change between tools and between months, so each step says what you are trying to achieve and what you should see when it worked. Your instructor names the specific tools by email one week before session 1.
If a step fails, do not guess. Copy the sentence in “Ask the assistant” and paste it, with the error message, into your assistant.

title: Toolkit setup guide
section: The tools and what each is for
text:
The tools and what each is for








Tool
What it is for
You will recognize it by




An AI assistant that supports skills, connectors and agents
Thinking, drafting, and later building in your repository
A chat window that can also open a folder of files and act on it


An app builder
Your first version, from a sentence to a deployed app
You describe the app and it appears, with a “Publish” button


GitHub
The home of your app’s files, with every version kept
A website where each project is a “repository”


A managed database and a hosting platform
Where the data lives, and where the public address comes from
Dashboards with a project name, keys and a web address


A model provider’s developer account (from session 3)
The model your app calls, billed by use
A console with usage, a spending limit and API keys



Expected cost for the course: USD 45 to 60 per student: two months of the assistant’s individual plan and about USD 5 to 10 of model usage. Confirm the current prices before you pay; they change.

title: Toolkit setup guide
text:
The data rule
Until your team has completed the session 4 lab, closed every critical finding, and has the written agreement of the organization that owns the data, use only invented or de-identified information: no real names, phone numbers, addresses or tax numbers. Most teams will stay with de-identified data through Demo Day, and that costs nothing in the grade. A realistic message with the names, phone numbers and addresses changed teaches you exactly as much as the real one.

title: Toolkit setup guide
text:
Before session 1 (about 20 minutes, every student)

Create an account on the AI assistant named by your instructor, on the individual paid plan if the free plan does not include skills and connectors.
Create an account on the app builder. The free tier is enough for session 1.
Create a GitHub account. Use a personal email you will keep after the course.
Write down the one business problem you will bring: who has it, how often, and what it costs them.

title: Toolkit setup guide
text:
Before session 2 (about 75 minutes)
In session 1 you built a first version inside the app builder. Before session 2 you move it to a place where your assistant can work on it properly, and you prepare the database.
Who does what. Parts A, C and D are done once per team, by the member whose builder account holds the app. Part B is done by every member, on their own laptop. Do the parts in order.

Part A. Put the app in a private repository (10 minutes, once per team)
Goal: the files of your app live in a GitHub repository that only your team can see.

In the app builder, open your project and find the option to connect to GitHub or export the project. It is usually in the project settings or behind a GitHub icon.
Allow the builder to create a repository in your GitHub account. Name it after your product, for example quotedesk.
Open GitHub in your browser, find the new repository, open its settings, and confirm its visibility is Private. If it says Public, change it now.
In the repository settings, invite your teammates as collaborators.

It worked when: you can see a list of files in the repository on GitHub, a small padlock or the word “Private” sits next to its name, and your teammates can open it.
Ask the assistant: “I am not a programmer. I built an app in [builder name] and I need its files in a private GitHub repository. Tell me exactly where to click, one step at a time, and wait for me to confirm each step.”


Part B. Open the repository in your assistant (30 minutes, every member)
Goal: your assistant can read and change the files of your app on your own laptop.

Install the desktop version of your assistant, or the editor your instructor named, on your laptop.
Sign in to GitHub from inside it when it asks.
Choose the option to open a repository from GitHub (it may be called “clone”, which means download a linked copy), pick your repository from the list, and choose a folder on your laptop to keep it in.
Ask the assistant: “Describe this project to me in five sentences. What does it do, what are its main parts, and how do I run it on my laptop to see it?”
Follow its instructions to run the app on your laptop. It will ask to install two free programs (Git and Node.js) and may ask for your computer password; say yes. Allow 30 minutes the first time. A browser tab opens with your app in it.

It worked when: the assistant describes your app correctly and you can see the app in a browser tab on your own laptop.
Ask the assistant: “I cannot see my app running. Here is what I see: [paste]. Fix it and tell me in one sentence what was wrong.”


Part C. Create the database project (15 minutes, once per team)
Goal: an empty database exists, ready for session 2. You do not design tables now.

Create an account on the managed database service named by your instructor and create a new project. Give it the same name as your product. Choose the region closest to your users.
The service shows you a project address and two keys. Read the section “Keys” below before you copy anything.
Put the project address and the publishable key in your project’s settings, following your assistant’s instructions (see “Ask the assistant” in the Keys section). The secret key waits for Part D.
Do not create tables. Your team does that together in the session 2 lab.

It worked when: you can see an empty project dashboard, your project’s settings hold the address and the publishable key, and no secret key is anywhere in the repository.


Part D. Connect the hosting platform (10 minutes, once per team)
Goal: every time your team saves a checkpoint, a public address updates by itself.

Create an account on the hosting platform named by your instructor, signing in with GitHub.
Choose “import a project” or “new project” and pick your repository.
Before you deploy, open the platform’s page for “environment variables” or “secrets” (settings stored on the server, outside the code) and add the database project’s address, its publishable key and its secret key there. This page is the only place a secret key is ever typed.
Accept the suggested settings and deploy. The platform gives you a public address.
Open that address on your phone.

It worked when: your app opens on your phone at an address you did not have yesterday, and the secret key appears in the hosting platform’s settings and nowhere else: no chat, no message, no file.


Part E. Five checks (10 minutes)

The repository is private, and every teammate can open it.
Every member's assistant can describe the project and run it on their laptop.
The database project exists and its secret key has not been pasted into any chat, message or file.
The hosting address opens on a phone.
You asked the assistant to make one small visible change (for example the page title), saved a checkpoint, and saw the change appear at the public address a minute later.

A checkpoint is a named snapshot of the whole app at a moment it worked. In this course, saving a checkpoint always includes sending it to GitHub, which is what updates your public address. Until then, a change exists only on one laptop.

title: Toolkit setup guide
section: Before session 3 (about 25 minutes, once per team)
text:
Before session 3 (about 25 minutes, once per team)
In session 3 your app calls a language model. That needs an account that is separate from your assistant subscription and is billed by use.

Create an account on the model provider’s developer console named by your instructor. Add USD 5 of credit.
Set a monthly spending limit of USD 10 and an email alert.
Create one API key (a secret key that lets your app use the model), name it after your product, and type it into your hosting platform’s environment variables page. Nowhere else.

It worked when: the key appears on the hosting platform’s page, the spending limit shows in the provider’s console, and the key is in no chat, message or file.
Because the key lives only on the hosting platform, the AI feature will not run on your laptop. In the session 3 lab you save a checkpoint, wait a minute for the public address to update, and test there.

title: Toolkit setup guide
section: For the morning digest (session 3, option B)
text:
For the morning digest (session 3, option B)
One of the two options in session 3 is a morning digest that your team’s assistant prepares on a schedule. The assistant cannot see inside your deployed app, so you hand it a file through the same door it already uses for the price list.

Ask the building assistant: “Add a manager-only button ‘Export pending requests’ that downloads a file with customer, time received and rep. No prices, no phone numbers.”
Save that file each morning into the shared folder your price-list connector already reads. In the lab you do this once by hand.
Ask your assistant one question that needs the file (“how many requests are older than three hours?”) and check the answer against the app.

It worked when: the answer matches what you see in the app, and the connector’s settings still show read access and nothing else.
A real deployment needs a view that refreshes by itself and a second alert channel. Note both as open items in your risk memo.

title: Toolkit setup guide
text:
Keys
A key is a long string that lets software use a service on your behalf. Treat it like the keys of a building.








Kind of key
Who may see it
Where it goes




Publishable key (the database service may call it “anon” or “public”)
Anyone. It is designed to reach the browser.
In the project’s settings, where the assistant puts it


Secret key (it may be called “service” or “secret”; the key of the model provider is always secret)
Nobody outside the server
On the hosting platform’s “environment variables” or “secrets” page, and nowhere else



Three rules that are never broken:

A secret key is never pasted into a chat, an email, a slide, a screenshot or the repository.
If a secret key was ever pasted somewhere it should not be, it is revoked in the service’s dashboard and a new one is created. Deleting the message is not enough.
The publishable key does not protect your data. The rules inside the database do. You set the first rules in session 2, with the login, and tighten and test them in session 4.

Ask the assistant: “I have a publishable key and a secret key for [service]. Tell me exactly where each one goes in this project and in [hosting platform], and confirm that the secret key will never be sent to the browser. Do not ask me to paste the secret key into this chat.”
